hero.rubrik: 5 reasons RV owners skip a roof cover, and what happens to the roof instead.
hero.ingress: If your rig sits through the winter with nothing on the roof, you probably have a reason. We've heard a lot of them, and five come back more than the rest. Here they are in order, with what the roof gets while the reason stands, and a straight answer to each one, or an honest 'we don't know' where that's the truth.
hero.knapp: See the cover → nine lengths, from $199
sammanfattning: The five reasons, in the order we hear them: nothing in the pictures looks like their roof, the price they saw wasn't the price for their rig, the last cover they owned did more harm than good, for that money they'd rather wrap the whole RV, and nobody they know has one. Each gets its answer below.

The cover itself: black 210D Oxford, waterproof and sun-resistant, nine lengths from 18 to 44 ft, all 10 ft wide, from $199 for one. Woven webbing straps on all four sides, one person to put it on, free shipping to the US in 5 to 10 business days, and 90 days to send it back or get a refund.

pristabell.rubrik: Your length, your price, before you click anything
pristabell.text: Every size is 10 ft (3 m) wide, so the only thing to measure is the length: the body, hitch not included, rounded up to the next size when you land between two. One cover costs what its row says. On the product page the bundle box opens on a 2-pack, so with one RV, switch it to 1 pack and you pay the row.
pristabell.fot: Nothing here is shorter than 18 ft or wider than 10 ft. A smaller rig, or a wider one, needs a different cover, and we'd rather lose the sale than your trust.

punkter.rubrik: 1. Nothing in the cover pictures looks like their roof.
punkter.text: Roof-cover ads, ours included, tend to show the same thing: a long, flat, empty roof. A real American travel trailer carries a rooftop A/C unit, a couple of vent hoods and a plumbing stack, and the owner who looks at that smooth roof in the picture, then at his own, decides the cover was made for somebody else. So the roof stays bare, and the rain sits around the very hatches and seams a cover is supposed to keep it away from. Here is what we can tell you, and only that. The cover is a flat sheet of waterproof fabric, 10 ft wide, in nine lengths up to 44 ft. It lies over whatever is on the roof, and the straps hook under the edge of the body on all four sides. How it sits over an A/C unit, and whether the unit costs you a size, we don't have the maker's answer on, so we won't make one up. What you get instead is 90 days: put it on, look at how it sits over your A/C, and if it doesn't work, it goes back.
punkter.knapp: See the cover → 90 days to try it on your roof

punkter.rubrik: 2. The price they saw wasn't the price for their rig.
punkter.text: The ad says $199, and $199 is true, for the shortest cover. Your rig is probably longer than 18 ft, and when you click through, the cart says more than the ad did. That's the moment a fair price starts to feel like bait, and the tab gets closed. The roof, meanwhile, gets another winter of weather with nothing on it. So the whole price list sits on this page, above this text, one row per length: $199 for 18 and 21 ft, and up to $389 for the 44-footer. Every row has its own button that opens exactly that size, so the number you see up there is the number you pay for one cover. If the price for your length is more than a roof is worth to you, that's a fair call. It just shouldn't be a call about whether we're honest.
punkter.knapp: Find your length in the table → from $199

punkter.rubrik: 3. The last cover they owned did more harm than good.
punkter.text: Ask around on any storage lot and someone has a cover story: bungee cords that stretched out by February, plastic hooks that let go in the first storm, a cover that turned into a parachute, and marks along the sides where it rubbed. One bad cover teaches an owner to leave the roof alone, and after that the roof takes every winter with no protection at all, because a cover once failed him. That history is why the straps on this one are what they are. The maker's reason for using woven webbing instead of elastic is the same story: elastic loses its stretch over time, so they don't use it. There are straps on all four sides, adjustable, with hooks that latch under the edge of the body, and two reinforced straps on top of that, which go across the whole roof. The maker also says the straps will not damage the paint. We haven't tested that ourselves, so it stands here as their word, not ours. One thing you won't find here is a wind rating. Nobody has measured one, and a number nobody measured is worse than no number.
punkter.knapp: See the straps and hooks up close →

punkter.rubrik: 4. For that money, they'd rather wrap the whole RV.
punkter.text: It sounds like the obvious upgrade: if you're spending real money on a cover anyway, why not one that covers the sides and the wheels too? The catch is what a full-body cover asks of you every time it goes on. Two people, a wall of fabric hauled over every corner without snagging, and then a whole winter of that fabric flapping against the sides in the wind. Ask the owner of one how many winters it actually went on. This cover takes the opposite bet. It covers the roof only, because the roof is where the rain sits, at the hatches and along the seams, all winter long. One person unfolds it on the roof, hooks the straps under the edge on all four sides, pulls the two reinforced straps across, and climbs down. The sides stay open, and yes, that means the sides stay uncovered. If wrapping the whole rig is what you want, this isn't your product, and we won't pretend it is.
punkter.knapp: Cover the roof, leave the sides →

punkter.text: With a truck or a hitch, you can ask the guy three sites over what he thinks. With a roof cover from a store you've never heard of, you can't. There's no neighbor to ask, the reviews on the product page read like translations, and the price came out of a Facebook ad. So the sensible move looks like waiting, and waiting means the roof gets one more winter of weather while you make up your mind. Here is what we put on the table instead of a neighbor. The reviews are translations. No review on that page was written by an American, and we won't invent one. The full price list stands above this text so the number is out in the open before you click. Shipping to the US is free and takes 5 to 10 business days. And you get 90 days: if it doesn't fit your rig, doesn't work over your A/C, or you simply don't like it, tell us within 90 days and either the cover goes back or your money comes back. That's not a testimonial. It's a way to find out for yourself without betting the price of the cover on it.
punkter.knapp: Find out for yourself → 90 days, return or refund

fragor.rubrik: The questions we get most, answered short

lista.fraga: Does it fit a fifth wheel?
lista.svar: Measure the main flat part of the roof and pick your length from that. Whether the cover also reaches over the raised front above the hitch, we don't have the maker's answer, so we don't claim it.
The cover goes over them, so they're covered while it's on. If your batteries depend on the panels through the winter, this cover works against you, and we'd rather say so.

lista.fraga: Doesn't a cover trap moisture underneath?
lista.svar: It can. The fabric is waterproof, so little air moves under it. A spacer that lifts the cover off the roof is in the works, with no date and no price yet. Until then, lay something under it that keeps a gap, a pair of pool noodles down the center line does it, and wait for a dry day before it goes on.
Yes. The fabric is black 210D Oxford, made to shed water and take the sun.

It's sold for winter storage, and the product page says to brush off heavy wet snow when it builds up. A number for how much snow the fabric holds doesn't exist on our side, so you won't find one here.

lista.fraga: Can one person really put it on?
lista.svar: Yes. It unfolds from the middle of the roof toward both ends, then the hooks catch under the edge and the two long straps cross the top. Doing the whole job from a ladder, without setting foot on the roof, is not something we can vouch for.

lista.fraga: Can I order two different lengths?
lista.svar: Yes. In the bundle box each cover gets its own size, so two rigs of different lengths fit in one order.
Free to the US, and 5 to 10 business days to your door.

lyckas.rubrik: So what do the people who do cover the roof do differently?
stycken: They stop waiting for the perfect cover and buy the one they'll actually put on. Length off the table, bundle box set to 1 pack, and the 90 days treated as a test drive rather than a warranty: on goes the cover before the first real rain, and the day it turns out the A/C or the straps make it wrong for their rig, back it goes.

The box holds one cover in the length you picked: black 210D Oxford that sheds rain and takes the sun, 10 ft across, woven webbing straps on all four sides with hooks for the edge of the body, and two reinforced straps for the top. When the season ends it folds small enough to carry under one arm. It ships free to the US in 5 to 10 business days, and it comes with the one thing we can actually promise: 90 days to return it or get your money back.
lyckas.knapp: Get the one you'll actually put on → from $199

stycken: this cover isn't for every rig. Shorter than 18 ft or wider than 10 ft, and none of the nine sizes fit, so keep your money. Parked somewhere damp with no way to leave a gap under the cover, and you're better off waiting for the spacer. And if you want the sides and the wheels wrapped too, buy a full-body cover from someone who makes one.

There are also three things about it we don't know: the rooftop A/C, the raised front of a fifth wheel, and how much snow it holds. We don't have the maker's answer on any of them, and an honest gap beats a confident guess.

Last, the price. It's set by length, from $199 at 18 and 21 ft to $389 at 44 ft, and the table above is the price for one cover. The bundle box on the product page opens on a 2-pack, so if you own one rig, click it down to 1.

riskfritt.rubrik: That's why you can try it risk-free.
riskfritt.text: Read your length off the table, or open the product page and pick it there. Then let the 90 days do the deciding. Wrong size, wrong roof, wrong idea, whatever the reason, tell us within 90 days and either the cover comes back to us or the money goes back to you. Shipping to the US costs you nothing.

lasbarhetstest.metod: Every paragraph read aloud as an RV owner on a storage lot would hear it, the six points from /lagerrensning: each sentence picks up where the last one left off, mixed sentence length, at most one 'Not X. Y.' device per paragraph, one paragraph = one thought moving forward, words people use on the lot (rig, travel trailer, motorhome, fifth wheel, rooftop A/C, vent hoods, hitch, bundle box, storage lot, the guy three sites over), and the whole page read top to bottom as one person talking through five reasons. Order = US comment counts in the report (A/C 23, size and price 16, trust 10, straps 6, whole-RV 5), with the trust reason placed last because the /anledningar skeleton ends on price logic and the guarantee. Every reason runs the same arc: the reason people skip the cover → what the roof gets while the reason stands → the honest answer → the flip into a reason to switch. Nothing on the page says 'you wrote' or 'one of you asked' (Axel's brief: not so obviously answering the comments), and nothing says 'we've asked the maker' (no question has been sent).
lasbarhetstest.omskrivna_stycken: Ingress: the first draft opened 'Most rigs on a storage lot sit through the winter bare' — a statistic nobody measured, rewritten to address the reader ('If your rig sits through the winter with nothing on the roof, you probably have a reason'). Point 1: 'Every roof-cover ad shows the same thing' — 'every' softened to 'tend to, ours included', which is also more honest about our own pictures. Point 2: cut 'nobody who owns an 18-footer shops in the same numbers as the people with a 32 or a 39' (a demographic claim) and 'most rigs on the road are longer than 18 ft' (unsourced); now 'your rig is probably longer than 18 ft'. Point 3: the maker quote, the paint sentence and the wind sentence rewritten so no sentence is shared with the sister page rv-roof-cover-before-you-buy; 'bungee cords … plastic hooks … parachute … marks' are the four failures the comments name. Point 4: 'plenty of those covers spend their second winter in the garage' (a count) → 'ask the owner of one how many winters it actually went on'; 'every awning arm' cut as needless detail; 'a few hundred dollars' → 'real money' so the page carries no price but the product's. Point 5: the double 'and' in the reviews sentence split into two sentences; the closing button changed from the sister page's 'Try it for 90 days'. Lyckas, arlig and riskfritt rewritten twice so they share no sentence with the sister page (same product, same store — /listiclar's rule: different copies, no shared sentence). Numbers written as Americans say them: 18-footer, 44-footer, 10 ft, 5 to 10 business days, no dash ranges in prose.
lasbarhetstest.kvar_att_lyssna_pa: Point 5's closer, 'It's a way to find out for yourself without betting the price of the cover on it.' — the longest thought on the page and the one that might read as clever rather than plain aloud; alternative: 'It's a way to find out without losing the money.' Also the table footnote 'we'd rather lose the sale than your trust' — if it sounds like a slogan, cut to 'and we'd rather say so here than in a return email'.
